title: Automatic gate opener: actuator arms, gear motor, batteries and safety beams
summary: A gate opener gives you 24 V linear-actuator arms or a worm-geared DC gear motor, two 12 V backup batteries, a 24 V transformer, limit switches, an infrared beam pair, a remote receiver and sometimes a solar panel. Allow about 45 minutes. The dangers are the mains wiring in the control box and the gate itself, which can swing or roll free once its drive is off.

steps.text: Look before you touch. Work out which kind it is: swing-gate arms (a telescoping or screw arm from a post to each gate leaf), or a sliding-gate unit (a box on a concrete pad with a toothed rack on the gate). Open the control box and see how it is powered: a mains cable from the building, a solar panel on a pole, or both.

Make the gate safe first. Put it where you want it, usually closed, and hold it: chock the wheels of a sliding gate, tie or wedge each swing leaf. If you need to move the gate by hand, use the manual release key or lever on the opener. Once the drive is released or removed, a leaf can swing in the wind or roll away downhill.
steps.warn: A heavy gate that rolls or swings free can crush hands, feet and legs. Chock it before you take the drive off and stay out of its path.

steps.text: Cut the power. Mains-fed: switch off and tag the breaker or isolator that feeds the opener, then prove the control box terminals dead with a meter you have just checked (see safety_mains_isolation). Solar-fed: cover the panel with an opaque cloth first. Backup batteries come out in a later step.
steps.warn: A dead grid does not make it dead: a generator or a solar system can still feed the mains wires. If you can't find the supply or prove it dead, don't touch the mains wiring.

steps.text: Photograph the terminal block, then label every wire with tape: motor, limit switches, beams, lock, aerial, mains in, battery. A phone photo does not survive a flat battery; sketch it too.

Take the backup batteries: usually two 12 V 7 Ah sealed lead-acid batteries joined in series for 24 V. Disconnect the negative lead first, then the positive, tape the ends and lift them out (about 2 kg each). Check them later with test_lead_acid.
steps.warn: A short across a sealed lead-acid battery melts tools and starts fires. Keep metal off the terminals.

steps.text: Take the transformer, the control board and the remote receiver. With the mains proved dead, undo or cut the mains leads at the transformer, leaving 10 cm tails, and tape the ends. Unscrew the 24 V transformer. Keep the control board whole, with its plugs and any small plug-in receiver board and aerial wire.

Take the safety beams, limit switches and lock: the two small infrared boxes on the posts either side of the opening (one sends, one receives), the magnet and sensor pairs for the limit switches (magnets on the arm or rack, reed or Hall sensors in the base), and the 12/24 V electromagnetic lock if there is one. Keep each with its cable and plug.

Swing-gate arms: support the arm with one hand or ask a helper to hold it, pull the clip and pin at the gate end, then the post end. Keep the pins and brackets. Disconnect the motor cable in the control box and pull or cut it, leaving a long tail. Don't try to pull the arm apart: the screw and nut inside are meant to stay in the tube.
steps.warn: A dropped arm weighs about 8 kg and the free end swings. Hold it as the last pin comes out.

steps.text: Sliding-gate unit: undo the anchor nuts on the pad (usually four) and lift the gear motor out on its base plate, about 20 kg: two people (see safety_lifting). Unscrew the rack, the toothed steel or nylon bar along the gate; the screws are short and easy to lose. Keep the magnets that trip the limit switches.
Solar panel: lean the ladder so it can't slide, cover the panel with an opaque cloth, disconnect the two wires, then unbolt it. Keep the bracket and the wire.
steps.warn: Don't climb with the panel under your arm. Lower it on a rope or hand it down.

steps.text: Test what you took. Run the motor or actuator from two 12 V batteries in series (24 V) through a 10-15 A fuse for a couple of seconds; swap the leads to reverse it. Stop before the end of travel on an actuator that has no built-in stop. A worm gearbox should turn smoothly and hold when you let go.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Gear motor with a worm gearbox.** A 24 V DC motor and a worm reduction gear: slow, strong and self-locking, so it holds a load with no power. Winch (build_motor_winch), hoist, door or hatch opener, solar tracker, rotisserie.
- **Linear actuators.** 24 V screw-drive arms with 300-500 mm of stroke. They push and pull hundreds of kilograms slowly: greenhouse vents, hatches, doors, a tilting tracker. Reverse the leads to reverse the arm.
- **Running 24 V parts from 12 V.** They run at half speed with less force. Good enough for a lot of light jobs and gentler on the gearbox.
- **Backup batteries.** 12 V 7 Ah sealed lead-acid: alarms, lights, a radio.
- **24 V transformer.** Small mains transformer for 24 V DC or AC supplies. Check it with test_transformer before you use it.
- **Beam pair.** An infrared sender and receiver on cables: a tripwire for build_perimeter_alarm, a counter, a door sensor.
- **Magnets and reed or Hall sensors.** Contactless limit switches.
- **Remote receiver.** Learns only its own handset and uses rolling codes: of little use apart from its original remotes.
- **Rack.** Steel or nylon toothed bar: gear stock for a sliding mechanism.
- **Solar panel.** 10-40 W: a small 12 V charger (test_solar_panel).

## Before you strip it

- A working opener may protect someone's home or animals. If the gate is in use and the place is lived in, leave it running.
- Many are fine and only need a battery: check the batteries first.

## Variations

- Some openers run on 120/240 V mains motors, not 24 V. Read the label; treat the motor leads as mains (safety_mains_isolation).
- Underground and overhead (garage-style) operators have the same parts. Garage door springs are dangerous: see safety_garage_spring.
